claims.text: A conventionally processed W–Cu composite has direct tungsten–copper contacts.
Ultrathin, conformal silver coatings can be integrated between the tungsten and copper phases during fabrication.
Nanoscale silver interlayers reduce thermal resistance at W/Cu interfaces.
Nanoscale silver interlayers enhance bonding between tungsten and copper.
Silver has high intrinsic thermal conductivity.
Silver interlayers bridge W/Cu contacts and improve heat transfer across those interfaces.
Silver-induced improvement of interfacial bonding may help the composite sustain mechanical loads.
Silver-induced improvement of interfacial bonding may retard irradiation-induced degradation.
A W–Cu composite with silver interlayers will have significantly higher overall thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite without silver interlayers.
The mechanical strength of the silver-modified composite will remain at least equivalent to that of the baseline W–Cu composite.
The irradiation resistance of the silver-modified composite will remain at least equivalent to that of the baseline W–Cu composite.
The predicted benefits will hold under high-temperature operation and fusion-reactor-level irradiation.
The beneficial effect depends on the silver layers being continuous.
The silver layers must be sufficiently thin to avoid separate-phase formation or composite embrittlement.
Performance may vary when silver-layer thickness or distribution is not well controlled.
Direct evidence for the longevity and stability of ultrathin silver coatings under fusion-reactor irradiation is limited.
